newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sony's PlayStation seen prevailing over rivals.
newsitem.headline: Sony's PlayStation seen prevailing over rivals.

text.p: Sony Corp is likely to continue pummeling its rivals in the battle for the home videogame market, despite the planned merger of one of its chief rivals, analysts say.

Armed with commitments from developers of Japan's most popular game software, Sony's PlayStation is seen keeping its edge over rival machines from Nintendo Co and another leading videogame maker, Sega Enterprises Ltd.
Sega and toymaker Bandai Co Ltd on Thursday announced plans to merge in Ocober.

Although a latecomer to the market, PlayStation currently holds nearly a 50 percent share in the worldwide market for game machines of 32 bits or more, while Sega and Nintendo respectively hold 32.3 percent and 18.0 percent.
"One of the reasons that PlayStation has been selling so briskly is that it offers a wide variety of games," said Masahiro Ono, an analyst at Credit Lyonnais Securities.
PlayStation's market dominance is likely to be reinforced by its success in the past year in luring major software houses to its camp, analysts said.

Japanese software maker Enix Corp announced earlier this month that it would develop the latest version of the game "Dragon Quest VII" for Sony's 32-bit PlayStation game console. The software house had previously developed Dragon Quest games only for industry leader Nintendo's 16-bit Super Famicom.
In early 1996, another game software house, Square Co Ltd, said it would develop the seventh version of its mainstay "Final Fantasy" game to run on the PlayStation.
As with Dragon Quest, earlier versions of Final Fantasy, one of Japan's best-selling game titles, had been supplied only to Nintendo.
"The software makers' moves were decisive in making PlayStation the market leader," said Yutaka Sugiyama, senior analyst at UBS Securities Ltd.
Software houses were lured to the Sony camp in part because it is far cheaper to develop games for the PlayStation platform than for Nintendo64.
Although Nintendo's 64-bit machine is smarter and faster than the current mainstay 32-bit machines, it also requires software developers to use more advanced workstation computers, analysts said.
Sony's aggressive thrust into the market was cited as one factor forcing Sega to seek a merger partner that could help it become more competitive.
"This merger probably reflects the sense of crisis over Sony's growing videogame market dominance," said one analyst.
Since its launch in December 1994, Sony's 32-bit PlayStation console has outsold its chief rivals -- the 64-bit Nintendo64 and Sega's 32-bit Sega Saturn -- both at home and abroad.
As of the end of last year, Sony had sold a cumulative total of five million PlayStations in Japan and another six million units in the United States and Europe.
Total sales of Sega Saturn, which hit the market shortly before PlayStation's launch, have so far reached 4.4 million in Japan and 2.76 million overseas.
Nintendo64 racked up sales of 1.85 million units domestically and 2.14 million overseas since it was launched in June 1996.

While many analysts said the Sega-Bandai merger posed little threat to Sony's growing grip on the game player market, some said the newly merged company may have a head start in the race with Sony and other rivals to profit by linking television, videogames and the Internet.
"The merger will provide Sega certain competitiveness in next-generation game machines," said an analyst at a foreign brokerage in Tokyo.
